slides.0.title: Regulations in Depth and Reading Labels
slides.0.subtitle: The Côtes du Rhône family and IGPs
slides.1.title: Naming tiers and how labels are written
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The pyramid on the label
slides.1.highlights.0.content: 'Côtes du Rhône' → 'Côtes du Rhône Villages' → 'Côtes du Rhône Villages + place name' → a cru appears under its own name (for example Gigondas). The wording on the label is direct evidence of the tier
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Villages + name is still Villages
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The 21 names that may be added (for example Plan de Dieu, Sablet) remain within the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC; a cru is an independent AOC and no longer carries 'Côtes du Rhône Villages' on the label
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Label changes after promotion
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Before 2016 Cairanne could appear as Côtes du Rhône Villages Cairanne and since then it is a cru; 2024 is Laudun's first cru vintage. When reading a vintage, check the label wording as well
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Do not read just one word
slides.1.highlights.3.content: 'Rhône', 'Côtes du Rhône' and 'Côtes du Rhône Villages' differ by a word or two, yet proportions, area and yield rules all differ; exams use this as a trap
slides.1.content: Reading order: find the name first (cru or Côtes du Rhône family), then 'Villages' and the place name, and finally vintage and bottler.
slides.2.title: Proportion rules and the 'unit of calculation' trap
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Côtes du Rhône
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Grenache ≥30% (exception north of the Montélimar parallel), Syrah + Mourvèdre ≥20% (producing vines from the 2022 harvest), main varieties (Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre) together ≥70% (INAO, September 2018 version)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Villages
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Grenache ≥40%, Syrah + Mourvèdre ≥25%, main varieties ≥80%: stricter than Côtes du Rhône and limited to the south
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Calculated on whole-estate plantings
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The proportions are measured on the estate's total plantings (encépagement), not on each bottle's blend. In answers write 'estate plantings', not 'the blend of every bottle'
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Draft figures that are not examined
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Côtes du Rhône yield 51 hl/ha (cap 60) and minimum alcohol 11% (10.5% in the north); Villages yield 44 hl/ha (41 with a name) and 12% (12.5% for some reds). Most come from revision drafts or single sources, so they are noted but not examined
slides.2.content: Formula for proportion answers: give the figure + 'estate plantings' + the applicable date (from the 2022 harvest).
slides.3.title: IGPs and Vin de France
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Where IGP sits
slides.3.highlights.0.content: IGP (Indication Géographique Protégée, PGI in English) is the EU's middle tier and the successor of Vin de Pays. Its rules are looser than AOP, letting producers choose varieties and styles outside AOC specifications
slides.3.highlights.1.title: IGPs around the Rhône
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Former Vins de Pays listed in the Inter Rhône glossary include Gard, Vaucluse, Méditerranée, Ardèche, Drôme, Coteaux de l'Ardèche, Comté de Grignan, Principauté d'Orange, Aigues, Coteaux de Montélimar, Collines rhodaniennes and Coteaux des Baronnies (Méditerranée covers several départements)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Why producers choose IGP
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Common motives: planting varieties or plots outside AOC specifications, more yield flexibility, or selling under a variety name; the cost is losing AOC prestige (general account; the variety and yield rules of each IGP were not individually checked and are not examined)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Vin de France
slides.3.highlights.3.content: France's category without a geographical indication, yet the label may state variety and vintage (EU rules). It can be blended from different regions and is used for branded value wines and experimental cuvées
slides.3.content: When answering tier questions, treat AOP, IGP and Vin de France as three different regulatory tools with different protection, freedom and market positioning.
slides.4.title: Label-reading practice
slides.4.highlights.0.title: 'Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu'
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Villages with an added name (one of the 21); not a cru. Inference: estate rules of Grenache ≥40% and Syrah + Mourvèdre ≥25%, southern Rhône, mid-priced
slides.4.highlights.1.title: 'Cairanne'
slides.4.highlights.1.content: An independent cru (since 2016) with no 'Côtes du Rhône Villages' on the label. 'Côtes du Rhône Villages Cairanne' on pre-2016 bottles reflects the status before promotion
slides.4.highlights.2.title: 'IGP Collines Rhodaniennes Syrah'
slides.4.highlights.2.content: IGP tier with the variety named; an IGP associated with the northern Rhône valley, and it cannot carry an AOC name (the variety can be shown on IGP labels, but each IGP's rules were not individually checked)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: 'Vin de France Grenache 2022'
slides.4.highlights.3.content: No geographical indication, but variety and vintage are allowed; it cannot be assumed to belong to any Rhône AOC. Use price, alcohol and bottler to judge style
slides.4.highlights.4.title: Bottling information and 'old vines'
slides.4.highlights.4.content: 'Mis en bouteille au domaine / au château' means estate-bottled whereas 'négociant' signals bought-in fruit or wine; 'Vieilles vignes' has no uniform legal age in most AOCs and depends on each specification (general account)
slides.4.content: Practice method: cover the price and answer 'tier, likely proportion rules, style and price level' from the wording alone.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
A label reading Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu means?
A. An independent cru
B. Villages with an added name, still within the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC
C. An IGP wine
D. Vin de France
Plan de Dieu is one of the 21 names that may be added; a cru is the independent AOC.
On what basis are the Côtes du Rhône Grenache and Syrah + Mourvèdre minimums calculated?
A. The actual blend of every bottle
B. The estate's total plantings (encépagement)
C. The appellation-wide average
D. Only the grapes of the harvest year
The INAO specification measures estate plantings, so the blend of a single wine can differ from the overall proportions.
What may a Vin de France label do?
A. Show an AOC name
B. Show a village name and Premier Cru
C. Show neither variety nor vintage
D. Carry no geographical indication but may show variety and vintage
Under EU rules Vin de France has no geographical indication but may show variety and vintage.
Which is the correct way a cru appears on a label?
A. Côtes du Rhône Villages Gigondas
B. Gigondas (on its own as the AOC name)
C. IGP Gigondas
D. Vin de France Gigondas
A cru is an independent AOC and uses its own name, without 'Côtes du Rhône Villages'.
